Subject: Exploring dedicated reservation options + expected workload (LakeMind)

Hi David,

Thanks for taking the call earlier. Per our discussion, LakeMind is evaluating a Dedicated reservation to support two main workloads:
- Low-latency multi-turn chat (customer-facing assistant) ~ target p95 <= 150ms
- High-throughput embedding pipeline for nightly indexing (10k embedding requests/day, spikes during business hours)

Current baseline: avg 20 QPS sustained for chat, periodic bursts to ~60 QPS for short windows; model family will likely be a Llama-class open model (we're finalizing exact variant).

Key asks:
- Minimum committed GPU footprint you recommend for a safe onramp + a realistic ramp schedule to peak demand
- How you handle warm pools/prewarm and burst capacity
- Typical lead time from signature to warm GPUs available in US-East
- Any activation credits or warmup credits you can include for a pilot

I've attached a simple usage summary (lakemind_usage_summary.xlsx) that has our current QPS and token distribution.

Can you propose a few concrete reservation options and the tradeoffs? Procurement noted we may need a proposal they can take to finance.

Best,
Elena

Subject: Re: Exploring dedicated reservation options + expected workload (LakeMind)

Elena — thanks for the detail and the spreadsheet, that's very helpful. High level, I recommend we present three differentiated reservation packages so Procurement has clear choices. Below are pragmatic, numbered options with the operational tradeoffs you asked for. I've attached a short pricing/terms draft (dedicated_pricing_v2.pdf) for accounting.

1) Pilot (low-risk onramp) — Minimum: 8 H100-equivalent GPUs (dedicated), burstable to 16 via shared burst pool.
   - Use case: Proof-of-concept, 4-week canary, validate p95 targets and KV-cache behavior.
   - Warm pool: 2 GPUs prewarmed for fast cold-starts.
   - Ramp: immediate activation, validate in 1–2 weeks; option to convert to Scale or add more GPUs.
   - Tradeoffs: limited sustained throughput; good for latency validation and prompt engineering.

2) Scale (recommended mid-tier) — Minimum: 32 H100-equivalent GPUs dedicated.
   - Use case: Production small fleet — supports ~20–25 sustained QPS with headroom for growth.
   - Ramp: phased: 16 -> 32 over 2 weeks, with traffic shifting after successful canary.
   - Burst: 20% burst allowance via shared pool and autoscale policy.
   - Warm pool: configurable (default 8 GPUs).

3) Enterprise (high-availability runway) — Minimum: 128 GPUs dedicated, staged over 6 months.
   - Use case: full production, consistent high throughput and priority capacity.
   - Ramp: 32 -> 64 (month 1), 64 -> 128 (months 2–6) with defined milestones.
   - SLA: higher uptime SLA and reserved burst lanes, dedicated engineer on onboarding.

Operational notes and levers:
- Kernel & model variant: We'll select kernels and a quantization profile for the chosen model family to match your latency targets.
- KV cache and prefix-caching: We'll enable prefix caching for chat to reduce per-token work; this reduces required GPU count for the same p95.
- Autoscaling and fallback: We'll configure autoscale thresholds + a fallback route to a gen-quantized hosted variant (lower cost, slightly higher latency) in case of saturation.
- Lead time: For H100-equivalent capacity in US-East, typical activation lead time post-signature is 10–14 business days for the Pilot or Scale lanes; Enterprise phasing requires a brief capacity reservation and a 3–6 week coordination window for larger tranche activations.
- Credits: We can include a 2-week warmup credit for the Pilot tier to cover prewarming and initial tuning.

Next steps I propose:
- Confirm target p95 and whether you want strict hard-SLA guarantees in the SOW (affects price and minimums).
- Tell us your preferred GPU type (A100 vs H100) or we can recommend H100 if low latency and high throughput are priorities.
- If you want, Ben can build an initial Mutual Action Plan and Marissa can draft an SOW around the selected tier.

I've attached the draft pricing/terms for Procurement to review. Happy to jump on a short follow-up to walk through tradeoffs.

Thanks,
David

Thanks David — helpful framing. A few clarifications from our side:
- Target p95: <= 150ms for chat (user-facing); for embedding jobs we care less about p95 but want predictable throughput during nightly windows.
- Sustained: ~20 QPS for chat, typical daytime spikes to 60 QPS for <10 minute windows (user events).
- Region: us-east preferred (primary customers on East Coast).
- GPU preference: LakeMind prefers H100 if pricing delta is reasonable.
- Activation timeline: Procurement needs explicit wording about lead times and what triggers activation for subsequent tranches (e.g., usage thresholds, calendar dates).

Procurement also asked whether you can guarantee a brief prewarm window for model tuning once the Pilot is active (they want this written into the SOW).

If you can update the proposal with: clear activation triggers, explicit 2-week warmup credit terms for the Pilot, and an approximate cost delta H100 vs A100, we can move this to internal review.

Best,

Subject: RE: Engineering sizing + phased activation plan for LB-4827

David / team / Elena —

Quick technical recommendation based on the workload profile in the attachment and Elena's clarified targets:

Summary proposal (technical):
- Canary (Pilot): 16 x H100-equivalent GPUs for 2 weeks (vs my earlier note of 8) — reason: your 60 QPS spikes and desire for p95 <= 150ms mean 8 is tight once we include embedding backfill windows. Start canary with 16, keep 4 GPUs as warm pool, test KV cache hit rates and prefix reuse.
- Short-term scale: After successful canary (metric gates: p95 <= 170ms under 20 QPS sustained, KV cache hit >= 45%), move to 48 GPUs over 2–4 weeks (step: 16 -> 32 -> 48). This supports sustained 20–30 QPS with burst headroom.
- Medium/long-term: 48 -> 96 GPUs over 8–12 weeks if traffic becomes steady at higher QPS or embedding batch sizes increase.

Operational controls:
- Burst coverage: Reserve 10–15% of committed capacity as a prioritized burst lane (dedicated burst tokens) so you avoid noisy-neighbor impacts.
- Autoscale cooldown: 90s default, max burst window 10 minutes to avoid sustained overprovision.
- Fallback routing: Configure a route to a quantized hosted model for overflow (cost-effective, acceptable latency degradation).
- Model kernel selection: For Llama-class, enable fused attention kernels and 4-bit quantization profiles for embeddings where acceptable.

Activation triggers for tranche expansion (for SOW text):
- Usage trigger: sustained 7-day avg CPU/GPU utilization > 65% AND observed p95 degradation > 10% versus baseline.
- Calendar trigger: customer can request next tranche activation with 14 business days' notice (subject to availability).
- Auto-trigger: vendor can propose tranche activation if monitored signals indicate risk to SLA; activation requires mutual sign-off in contract to auto-execute.

Warmup credit and tuning window: we recommend a 2-week warmup credit window to be explicitly called out in the SOW — this covers kernel tuning, batching adjustments, and initial KV-cache population runs.

Attachments: ramp_workflow_diagram.png; cost_estimate_breakdown.csv (ballpark cost deltas H100 vs A100 included).

Next steps / ask:
- Elena: confirm if LakeMind is comfortable starting the Pilot at 16 H100s. If yes, we'll produce the one-page MAP and the SOW language for Procurement.
- David/Marissa/Ben: I'll iterate on the exact GPU hours and cost buckets once procurement confirms H100 preference.

Thanks,
